title: The Sample Passed. Which Factory Will Make the Order?
seoTitle: The Sample Passed. Which Factory Will Make the Order?
excerpt: Connect an approved sample to the actual manufacturing site, outside processes and first production lot before an undisclosed route change becomes a delivery problem.
author: James

articleBody.text: A good sample answers a product question. It does not automatically answer a production-location question. Before releasing a large order, the buyer needs to connect that sample to the company, site, equipment and outsourced operations that will actually make the goods. Otherwise, the approved object can become a reference for a process that has never been examined.

This is not an argument against subcontracting. A specialist heat treater, coating shop or toolmaker may be essential to a sensible supply chain. The risk is an unrecorded change: the sample comes from one route, the production order follows another, and nobody has agreed which differences require another approval.
Start with the sample's travel history

Ask the supplier to reconstruct how the approved sample was made. Record its identifier, drawing revision, material batch, production date and the address where the relevant operations occurred. Separate the company that issued the invoice from the company that manufactured it. A trading office can legitimately arrange production; its office address should not become the manufacturing address by default.

For a molded part, the useful questions include which tool and cavity produced the sample, which press ran it, and whether material preparation or finishing took place elsewhere. For fabricated steel, the route might include cutting, welding, galvanizing and packing at different locations. Record the route that matters to the specified product, rather than requesting a vague declaration that everything is made in-house.

The result should be a short, usable production map. Each critical operation gets a named company, a physical site, a responsible person and a record linking it to the sample. If the supplier cannot reconstruct the sample route, treat that as an unresolved qualification question. It is not proof of fraud, but it is a poor foundation for assuming repeatability.
Put the production site inside the approval

[Volvo's published May 2021 purchasing conditions](https://www.volvogroup.com/content/dam/volvo-group/markets/master/suppliers/our-supplier-requirements/Volvo-General-Purchasing-Conditions-May-2021.pdf) provide a useful industrial example. They distinguish sample approval from continuing supplier responsibility and require written consent before production is relocated wholly or partly. These are Volvo's contractual provisions, not rules that automatically apply to another buyer's purchase order.

The practical lesson is to describe what the buyer is approving. An approval record can identify the part and revision, the sample, the manufacturing site and the critical outside processes. Then specify which proposed changes must be notified before implementation. A move to a second building, a replacement coating subcontractor and a change of material source need different technical reviews; a single box marked “factory approved” hides those differences.

Make the notification route workable. Name who receives the request, who can authorize it and what production must wait for a decision. Silence in an email thread should not become an accidental approval mechanism. The actual agreement must define the commercial effect of a change and any stop or release decision.
Follow a real lot through the new route

A video tour can help orient a buyer, but the stronger question is whether one identified production lot can be followed through the claimed route. Select a lot from the actual order. Ask for its work instruction, material identification, in-process checks, outside-process handover and final inspection record. The identifiers should connect across the records without relying on an explanation invented after the photographs arrive.

For an outsourced operation, ask what physically travels to the processor and what comes back. Does the delivery record identify the batch or only a total weight? Does the processor's record identify the order, relevant specification and date? Who checks incoming parts after the outside operation? A certificate with the right process name but no link to the delivered lot leaves the central question unanswered.

Photographs should serve this investigation. Request a contextual view and a readable detail tied to the same lot, rather than a folder of attractive machines. A current factory sign, tool identifier or operation sheet can help locate the evidence, but none should be treated as a substitute for the connecting records.
A move needs a first-production decision

[Lear's October 2023 supplier bulletin](https://www.lear.com/suppliers-bulletin/requirements-for-production-tool-transfer-moves) makes the operating problem unusually visible: its tool-move requirements address advance approval, shared tooling, production cover and approval before shipments from a new location. The bulletin extends the concern to processing, assembly and sub-supplier tool moves. Its automotive approval requirements are Lear-specific; copying the form is less important than understanding the interruption it controls.

For another buyer, the corresponding decision might be a witnessed trial, renewed dimensional checks, a material review or a first-lot inspection. Choose it according to the changed operation and the consequences of failure. Agree how accepted stock will cover the transition, how old and new lots will remain distinguishable, and what happens if the trial fails. A delivery date should not quietly erase the approval step.

Before production release, the purchasing and technical owners should be able to answer three questions together: where was the approved sample made, where will this lot be made, and which evidence establishes that the difference is acceptable? An openly managed second site can be qualified. An unnamed second site cannot be assessed simply because the sample on the desk looks right.

title: The Container Arrived Wet. More Desiccant May Be the Wrong Answer.
seoTitle: The Container Arrived Wet. More Desiccant May Be the Wrong Answer.
excerpt: Wet pallets, leaks, temperature changes and unpacking conditions need different responses. Diagnose the moisture route before buying a larger drying-agent dose.
author: James

articleBody.text: When cartons arrive soft or steel arrives spotted with rust, the next packing instruction is often simple: add more desiccant. That may be part of the answer. It is not a diagnosis. A drying agent cannot repair a leaking roof, reverse damage already caused by wet packaging or make every unloading condition safe for cold machinery.

The purchasing task is to discover where the water entered the system, what released it during transport and where it condensed. Treat the container, goods, pallets, inner packaging and destination handover as one moisture problem. Buying another bag without answering those questions can repeat the failure with a larger packing bill.
The water may have been loaded with the goods

Hapag-Lloyd's [container-packing guidance](https://www.hapag-lloyd.com/content/dam/website/downloads/press_and_media/publications/Container_Packing_Broschuere_engl.pdf), in its section on climatic stresses, identifies cargo, packaging and stowage materials among the moisture sources. It explains that temperature changes can produce condensation on the container structure or packaging, with dripping water damaging the load. A sound container is therefore not the same thing as a dry transport system.

Ask how the goods and packing were stored before stuffing. Were wooden supports kept outdoors? Were cartons exposed while the loading area was wet? Was equipment washed or tested with water before packing? These are investigation questions, not a presumption that any one operation caused the loss. The point is to identify a source that can be measured or corrected before the doors close.

Do not accept “the pallet looked dry” as a moisture record. Agree with the packaging specialist what must be measured, which method is suitable for the material, where readings are taken and what acceptance condition applies. A universal moisture limit copied from another cargo is a weak substitute for a product-specific packing specification.
Container sweat and cargo sweat are different handovers

The [IMO/ILO/UNECE CTU Code, Annex 3](https://www.hapag-lloyd.com/content/dam/website/downloads/local_info/HPL-CTU_CODE_OF_PRACTICE.pdf) describes moisture released by cargo and associated materials as temperatures vary, followed by condensation on a cooling roof. It also distinguishes cargo sweat: cold goods can collect condensation when exposed to warmer, humid air during unpacking. Those mechanisms can require different receiving arrangements.

That distinction matters when an importer changes only the supplier's packing instruction. An arrival problem may also involve the warehouse opening the protective wrapping immediately. Record destination temperature and humidity conditions, the condition of the goods before and after opening, and the sequence of unloading. A receiving plan should be agreed with the packaging specialist and consignee for the actual cargo and climate; “always ventilate immediately” is not a safe universal instruction.
A desiccant has a moisture budget

The same CTU Code warns that drying agents generally lack enough absorption capacity to rescue hygroscopic cargo that was not sufficiently dry when packed. GDV's [Container Handbook loss-prevention discussion](https://www.containerhandbuch.de/chb_e/scha/scha_10_03_07.html) likewise describes saturation and the importance of the protected enclosure. A small packet inside a product bag and a hanging unit inside an entire freight container are different arrangements.

The useful supplier question is not just how many bags were installed. Ask what enclosure the design protects, which moisture sources were included, what voyage and storage duration were assumed, and which capacity data support the selection under the expected conditions. Request installation instructions and a record showing the correct product was fitted in the specified positions without damage.

For sensitive machinery, discuss whether a properly designed barrier package is needed around the equipment. Its seams, penetrations and internal timber are part of that discussion. A bag inside an imperfect wrapping does not make the package vapor-tight. Neither a barrier nor a desiccant removes the separate need for cargo securing and a suitable unloading method.
Rule out liquid water before adjusting the dose

The handbook's separate section on [rainwater and leaks](https://containerhandbuch.de/chb_e/scha/scha_10_03_04_05.html) describes wetting during loading and damage that can allow water through roofs, floors or door areas. That is a different corrective action from increasing passive absorption. Request a documented container-condition check and loading-weather record, including defects found and the decision to accept or reject the unit.

At destination, preserve the pattern of damage before rearranging the load. Photograph the ceiling, doors, floor and representative packages; identify which faces were wet and where they sat. Keep the container and seal identifiers, loading photographs, packing-material records and available temperature or humidity logs together. Those observations support a technical investigation; they do not by themselves allocate liability between seller, packer and carrier.

For the next shipment, agree a change that can be checked: drier packing materials, a corrected container defect, a revised protective package or a better receiving sequence. Then state who verifies it before release. Desiccant can be a useful component of that plan. It should not be the explanation for every wet arrival or the only item the buyer negotiates.

title: The Mold Is Paid For. Can You Actually Move It?
seoTitle: The Mold Is Paid For. Can You Actually Move It?
excerpt: Compare the asset you own, the storage and care you receive, and the cost of the first accepted batch after a tool transfer—not just the mold charge.
author: James

articleBody.text: A tooling quotation can look complete while leaving the buyer's next sourcing decision undefined. The mold price is agreed, parts are being produced and the supplier says the tool belongs to the customer. Months later, moving production raises a different set of questions: which components can leave, who prepares them, what records travel with them and what the receiving factory must spend before making an acceptable part.

These questions belong in the original commercial discussion. Ownership, custody and practical portability are connected, but they are not the same promise. A useful quotation makes each one inspectable before the buyer becomes dependent on the tool.
Start with the asset, not the invoice label

Ask the supplier to define what the tooling price buys. Does it include a complete mold, cavity and core inserts, a shared mold base, hot-runner equipment, dedicated fixtures, spare components and gauges? Which items are supplier equipment that will remain behind? A short asset schedule with photographs and identifiers is more useful than an invoice describing everything as a “mold charge.”

Record the owner, the agreed ownership milestone and the entity holding the tool. If a third-party toolmaker will build or repair it, name that party and its location. Decide how the buyer will know where the asset is after a repair or transfer. These are terms to agree, not conclusions that can be drawn from the fact that a deposit was paid.

[Bosch's North American non-mobility purchasing terms, revised February 2026](https://assets.bosch.com/media/global/bosch_group/purchasing_and_logistics/information_for_business_partners/downloads/purchasing_docs/terms_and_conditions/americas/non-mobility-direct-and-indirect-purchasing-potc-for-north-america.pdf), illustrate how specifically an industrial buyer can address these subjects. Their property and tooling provisions cover identification, custody, maintenance, outside toolmakers and return. They are Bosch's contractual allocation, not a general entitlement available to every mold buyer or a statement that every clause is enforceable in every jurisdiction.
Storage is a service with an end date

A supplier can offer a low initial tooling price while attaching different conditions to future use. Protolabs' [published comparison of molding options](https://www.protolabs.com/services/injection-molding/on-demand-manufacturing/) explicitly distinguishes ownership and inactive-storage arrangements between its service options. This is a manufacturer's own offer, not an industry-wide tariff, but it shows why the buyer must compare the whole arrangement.

Ask when inactivity begins, how the supplier warns the buyer before storage ends and what happens if the buyer does not respond. Is extended storage chargeable? Who authorizes disposal? Are cleaning, corrosion protection and routine maintenance included, and how is their completion recorded? Specify a contact and a fallback contact; a tooling asset should not disappear because the original purchasing employee changed jobs.

Separate routine care from a design change or major repair. Request an approval process for work that changes cavity geometry, surface finish or critical components, together with a condition record and retained reference samples. Agree what the supplier must disclose before the next order is priced. “Lifetime maintenance” needs an operating definition if it is going to influence the sourcing comparison.
Quote the exit while everyone still wants the order

Ask for a transfer schedule alongside the production quotation. It should identify the notice period, inspection and release process, deinstallation responsibilities, lifting provisions, protective packing and transport handover. Ask whether there are charges for cleaning, dismantling, service work, packing, administration or outstanding agreed tooling amortization. Record what is included, what is excluded and how variable charges will be authorized.

Do not turn this into a demand that every possible future move must be free. The purpose is to make costs visible and avoid an undefined release condition. Commercial disputes, liens, intellectual-property rights and cross-border recovery can depend on the signed documents and applicable law. Have the actual arrangement reviewed for the relevant jurisdiction rather than copying a large customer's clause and assuming the problem is solved.

The receiving molder also needs a quotation. Provide tool dimensions and weight, mounting and service interfaces, runner and control details, drawings, material information, repair history and agreed reference parts. Ask it to identify required adaptations and the evidence needed to accept production. A transferable physical object may still need work before it fits the new process.
Price the first accepted batch at the new site

A sourcing comparison should include release and transport costs, incoming inspection, adaptations, trial material, testing and the inventory needed during transition. Keep uncertain amounts visible as allowances or items awaiting quotation. A precise-looking total built on unconfirmed assumptions can conceal more risk than an honest range.

Agree the acceptance milestone before the tool leaves. Who decides whether the receiving-site trial is acceptable, against which drawing revision and inspection plan? Which open defects must be resolved, and who owns the decision if the tool condition differs from the handover record? Tool release and production release should be separate decisions.

The strongest time to ask these questions is before awarding the mold. A slightly higher quotation with clear asset identity, care obligations and a workable exit may leave the buyer with a more useful sourcing option. The commercial value is not simply having an ownership sentence. It is being able to obtain another qualified source without discovering the transfer terms during the interruption.
